transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-12-09 15:00 UTC
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Alex Rivera (Redwood AE), Priya Nandi (Redwood SE), Samir Cho (Redwood SA), Jordan Lee (CTO, HelioStream), Maya Patel (ML Eng), Omar Ruiz (Infra), Nina Gomez (PM)

Summary:
Quick scoping call for a 4-week pilot to validate autoscaling, reserved GPU baseline with burst capacity, and graceful fallback policies. Discussed success criteria (p95 latency, cost per 1M tokens, QoR), workload sizing inputs, benchmark plan and timeline. Agreed next steps: send pricing, share bench harness, dry-run, and security docs.

Topics covered:
- Baseline reserved capacity sizing and buffer
- Burst strategy: reserved + ephemeral burst (cloud or spot)
- Fallbacks: model variants, queued requests, degraded responses
- Benchmarks: synthetic vs replay, trace capture format, key metrics
- POC timeline and acceptance criteria

Transcript body:
[00:00] Alex (AE): Okay everyone, thanks for joining. We'll kick off, um, the scope for the HelioStream pilot — focus is reserved GPUs, burst behavior and fallback. I think Alex is muted, sorry.
[00:18] Jordan (CTO): No worries. Hey all. Quick context: we run real-time summarization for streaming telemetry, typical bursts during business hours, and occasional spikes on deploys. Our main constraints are p95 latency under 250ms and predictable monthly cost.
[00:33] Priya (SE): Great. When you say p95 250, is that for a 512 token window or average?
[00:41] Maya (ML Eng): It's for our standard request — usually about 400 to 600 tokens generated, often 1-shot with a 512 prompt. We can provide seq-length histogram, currently average output ~420 tokens.
[00:55] Samir (SA): For sizing we need peak QPS and sustained QPS. Jordan, what are peaks like?
[01:03] Jordan: Normal is 20 qps sustained, peaks go to 180 qps for short bursts up to 3 minutes, maybe once or twice a week. During a batch release we saw 450 qps for ~30s but that was an anomaly.
[01:20] Priya: Good, that helps. Suggestion: for the POC we model three phases: baseline reserved capacity to handle steady 20 qps, a burst buffer to absorb 180 qps spikes, and an emergency overflow fallback for >200 qps.
[01:35] Omar (Infra): Our infra team prefers reserved capacity because of SLA and predictability. We are open to ephemeral cloud burst or remote dedicated nodes. Curious about cost delta.
[01:45] Alex: We'll run numbers — example configuration: 8 reserved A100-equivalent GPUs for baseline, burst pool of up to 16 ephemeral GPUs (preemptible/spot or Redwood burst) controlled by autoscaler with ramp-up guardrails. That is an initial guess, we'll refine after traces.
[02:04] Jordan: 8 GPUs seems reasonable as a starting point, but can you explain the ramp-up time? We can't afford 2s cold starts for KV cache, etc.
[02:13] Priya: Ramp-up is two parts: instance spin-up + model warm-up. Redwood's burst path can use pre-warmed model snapshots in fast pool to reduce warm-up. Expect 20-45s for model hot path depending on quant and model size, plus continuous batching to smooth per-token latency. We can also use partial routing to send only lower-latency requests to reserved nodes.
[02:34] Maya: If warm-up is ~30s, what's the strategy for user-facing requests during that window? Queue? Return degraded content?
[02:42] Priya: We recommend a multi-tier fallback: 1) route to compatible smaller model variant for a short period (e.g., quantized variant or 7B instead of 13B) 2) return a cached prefix/summary for repeat queries 3) last resort, queue with a short TTL and surface progress. Choice depends on QoR tolerances.
[03:00] Jordan: We need a clear SLA for fallbacks — degraded but still acceptable. Our product team will define acceptable QoR loss.
[03:08] Nina (PM): On that note, our success criteria for pilot: p95 latency <= 250ms for reserved baseline, during spikes p95 <= 700ms with fallbacks allowed, and cost per 1M tokens below our threshold. Also no more than 1% of requests timed out or failed.
[03:30] Alex: Perfect. We'll bake those into the POC acceptance.
[03:36] Omar: Security: VPC, SSO via SAML, KMS for key management. We need to understand Redwood's private deployment options.
[03:45] Samir: Redwood Private offers a customer VPC variant — control plane managed, data egress limited, KMS integration. For the pilot we can do a private peering so logs don't traverse public internet. We'll send the security deck.
[03:59] Jordan: Is SOC2 report available?
[04:02] Alex: Yes, we'll attach SOC2 summary and an ISO outline. Also include encryption at rest details and audit logs.
[04:10] Maya: Benchmarks — we want to run replay of production traces. What's your recommended harness?
[04:16] Priya: Two-stage approach: 1) replay the anonymized traces you provide into Redwood's bench harness to measure p50/p95/p99 latency, throughput, token/sec and cost. 2) Synthetic stress tests: sustained QPS at 1.5x baseline, repeated spikes to validate autoscaler. We'll provide a repo link and a brief script.
[04:35] Jordan: Do you support client side recording format? We currently have JSON Lines with request ID, prompt length, response tokens, and timestamp.
[04:44] Priya: That works — seq-length histogram + timestamped events are ideal. We'll add a small wrapper to map fields.
[04:51] Omar: For the POC, will we be using Redwood hosted or Redwood Dedicated? We prefer dedicated if possible for performance isolation.
[04:59] Alex: For the short pilot, we recommend a hybrid: Dedicated reserved baseline (customer-isolated pool) with Redwood-managed burst capacity (hosted or partner cloud) to test autoscale behaviors without heavy infra commitment. If it proves out, we can convert to a longer Dedicated contract.
[05:15] Maya: How will cost be reported? We need token-level cost and cost/call breakdown.
[05:21] Samir: Redwood Console provides token-level cost breakdown, per-model and per-route. For the POC we'll enable detailed logs and a weekly cost digest.
[05:29] Jordan: For the fallback model variants, do you have recommendations in terms of quality delta? We can't lose critical intent detection.
[05:37] Priya: We'll recommend two fallback levels: 1) a quantized version of your chosen model with minimal QoR regression 2) a smaller architecture (e.g., 7B) with faster latency but more possible regressions. We'll provide evaluation prompts and a small eval harness to measure quality drift.
[05:52] Nina: Timeline?
[05:55] Alex: Proposed POC timeline: Week 0 (this week) - finalize scope and access; Week 1 - data ingest + bench dry-run; Week 2 - run baseline and burst experiments; Week 3 - iterate on policies, fallback tuning; Week 4 - final report, handoff. So about 4 weeks.
[06:12] Jordan: That aligns with our launch window. We want the pilot complete by mid-Jan if possible.
[06:18] Alex: We'll aim for report by 2028-01-12 then.
[06:23] Maya: On metrics, besides latency and cost, we want QoR regression numbers: accuracy/intent precision on a 200-item eval set.
[06:32] Priya: We'll collect that during bench runs. We'll also track model rollout metrics in the Console.
[06:38] Omar: Anything else on autoscaler guardrails? We want limits so burst doesn't explode spend.
[06:44] Samir: We'll set autoscaler policies: max burst capacity cap, grace period, rate-of-scale-up limit (e.g., 2x per 30s), and a budget cap that triggers automatic fallback to smaller models when exceeded. We'll document suggested defaults in the runbook.
[07:02] Jordan: If spot instances are used for burst, what about preemption recovery?
[07:07] Priya: Redwood's burst pooling can include preemptible nodes but the autoscaler prefers healthy instances and keeps a small warm buffer. If preempted, traffic is routed to other pools and fallbacks kick in. We'll show failure injection during bench.
[07:20] Nina: Who's owner for runbook?
[07:23] Alex: Priya will own the POC runbook with inputs from Samir. Alex will own commercial terms.
[07:30] Jordan: Can you share an example SLA for the pilot? Not full legal terms, but operational targets.
[07:36] Alex: Yes, we'll send a pilot SLA doc: uptime target for the dedicated pool, p95 latency targets for baseline and burst modes, and incident response times.
[07:45] Maya: One more thing: we have data residency needs for EU customers. Will that be relevant for pilot?
[07:51] Alex: If you need EU region testing we'll mirror the bench in EU; for this pilot, primary region is us-east but we can run a limited EU run if needed.
[07:59] Jordan: Okay great. Let's recap next steps now.
[08:04] Alex: Recap: Redwood to send pricing and runbook, security docs; HelioStream to send traffic traces and QoR eval set; schedule bench dry-run; meet again after dry-run to validate numbers.
[08:15] Nina: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[08:18] Jordan: Thanks all. Looking forward to the dry-run.
[08:21] Alex: Thanks, we'll follow up with calendar invites.

Notes on transcription quirks: occasional speaker mislabel (Alex briefly marked as muted), some model names and acronyms transcribed awkwardly (KV cache sometimes "K V cash"), time stamps approximate.

Referenced artifacts / links:
- Bench harness repo: https://redwood.example.com/bench/heliostream (shared after call)
- Pricing draft spreadsheet: sent by Alex post-call
- Security pack: SOC2 summary and KMS integration doc (to attach)

POC acceptance criteria (explicit):
- Baseline p95 latency <= 250ms for reserved pool on standard requests (420 tokens avg)
- On bursts up to 180 qps, p95 <= 700ms with allowed fallbacks; fewer than 1% timeouts
- QoR regression <= 5% on 200-item eval when using fallback model variant
- Cost per 1M tokens under agreed threshold (TBD in pricing spreadsheet)
